title: Springfield Founding and Washington County Seat
summary: Washington County, the first county created by Kentucky's General Assembly in 1792, took Springfield as its seat in 1793; its 1816 courthouse still stands.
bodyMarkdown:
When Kentucky's first General Assembly met in 1792, the first new county it created was [Washington County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Washington_County,_Kentucky), named for [George Washington](/people/#george-washington). The rolling country it covered, between the Bluegrass and the knobs, had drawn settlers since 1776. Many came along the Wilderness Trace from Danville, and from 1785 Catholic families from Maryland arrived in numbers, giving the county some of the oldest Catholic parishes in Kentucky.

The county needed a seat. In 1793 Gen. Matthew Walton, a Revolutionary War veteran and legislator who owned more than 200,000 acres in the county, laid off a town on his land. It was called Springfield for the springs that rose around it. By 1800 the new seat counted [163 residents](https://grokipedia.com/page/Springfield,_Kentucky), small by later standards but among the larger towns in the young state.

The Lincoln family put down roots here too. [Abraham Lincoln](/people/#abraham-lincoln-capt), grandfather of the future president, came to this part of Kentucky in 1782. He was killed in 1786, and his widow and children later settled near Springfield. His son [Thomas Lincoln](/people/#thomas-lincoln) married Nancy Hanks in Washington County on June 12, 1806, and their marriage record is still kept at the courthouse. The couple soon moved to Elizabethtown in Hardin County, and their son Abraham was born in 1809 on a farm in what is now LaRue County.

Springfield grew as a farm-market town and court town. Lawyers, farmers, and travelers gathered on court days, and roads ran out toward Bardstown, Lebanon, and Perryville. In the fall of 1862, Union and Confederate armies passed through the county on their way to the Battle of Perryville.

## Kentucky today

The Washington County courthouse in Springfield was built in 1816. When the state historical marker was written in 1965, it was the oldest courthouse in Kentucky still in use as one. North of town, Lincoln Homestead State Park preserves the setting of the Lincoln family's Washington County years, with reconstructed cabins.
